stem: A consumer consumes only two goods. If good1 has income elasticity1.2, what is the income elasticity of good2?
answer: C:Less than1, assuming positive budget shares and an exhausted budget.
solution: Differentiating the budget identity at fixed prices givesw₁η₁+w₂η₂=1, withw₁+w₂=1 and both shares positive. Henceη₂=(1−1.2w₁)/(1−w₁)=1−.2w₁/(1−w₁)<1. It may even be negative.
hint: Income elasticities have a budget-share weighted average of one.

stem: A Keynesian economy has consumptionC=15+Y^0.5 and autonomous investment plus government spending585. Find equilibriumY.
solution: Goods balanceY=15+√Y+585 givesY=600+√Y. Sets=√Y≥0; s²−s−600=(s−25)(s+24)=0, so s25 andY625. The negative algebraic roots−24 cannot be a square root.
hint: Set s=√Y and discard the negative root.

stem: For a monopolist, marginal cost increases at every output. What happens to the profit-maximizing price?
answer: Under the usual smooth, interior, strictly downward-sloping monopoly demand and regular second-order conditions: B, price rises. Without these assumptions only weak monotonicity is assured.
solution: With fixed demand and a regular interior optimum, raising marginal cost moves the MR=MC intersection to lower output; strictly downward inverse demand then implies higher price. More generally, if new costs exceed old costs by an increasing function of output, the optimal output cannot increase. Strict price increase need not follow with kinks, discrete output or a flat inverse-demand segment, so an unqualified strict answer needs regularity assumptions. The source supplies none of those qualifications; its handwritten ticks are not an answer key.
hint: Track the output choice first, then use inverse demand to infer price.
notes: Regularity assumptions for the usual strict price-increase answer are not stated; mark for review before selecting an unconditional MCQ key.
options: How price changes depends on the demand curve

stem: If government taxes10% of a monopolist’s profit, the monopolist will…
solution: A proportional pure-profit tax changes the objective fromπ(q) to.9π(q). Multiplication by a positive constant preserves the maximizing output and price; it reduces after-tax profit rather than changing marginal incentives.
hint: Compare the before- and after-tax objective functions.

stem: Competitive petrol demandQ_D=100−2P_c and supplyQ_S=3P_s. (i) Find untaxed equilibrium. (ii) With tax1 per litre, find consumer price, supplier price, quantity and excess burden.
solution: Without tax,100−2P=3P givesP20,Q60. With taxP_c=P_s+1, solve100−2(P_s+1)=3P_s, givingP_s98/5=19.6 andP_c103/5=20.6. Quantity is294/5=58.8. The tax reduces quantity by1.2; excess burden is the triangle(1/2)·tax·quantity decline=.6. Consumers bear.6 of each tax rupee and producers.4.
hint: Use the tax wedge between the two prices.

stem: A consumer has U(x₁,x₂)=min(2x₁,x₂). (i) Describe an indifference curve. (ii) At prices5,10 and income100, find the optimal bundle. (iii) Price1 rises to8: decompose the change in good1 into income and substitution effects.
answer: Initial bundle(4,8); final(25/7,50/7). Good1 total effect−3/7, substitution effect0 and income effect−3/7.
solution: Utility levelu has kink at(x₁,x₂)=(u/2,u), with vertical and horizontal rays extending upward and rightward from the kink. Optimal quantities satisfy x₂=2x₁. Initially(5+20)x₁=100, so(4,8). With new price8,(8+20)x₁=100, so x₁=25/7 and x₂=50/7. Both Hicks and Slutsky compensation preserve the original kink bundle: its new expenditure is8·4+10·8=112. At compensated income112 the optimum remains(4,8), hence substitution effect is zero and the entire decline25/7−4=−3/7 is an income effect.
hint: Perfect complements retain the same optimal quantity ratio after a price change.

stem: In a simple open Keynesian model, investment and exports are autonomous. What happens toGDP and aggregate imports when the propensity to import rises?
answer: GDP falls; imports rise under the standard linear model.
solution: LetC=C₀+cY, exportsX̄, investmentĪ and imports=mY, with0<c<1,m>0. DefineA=C₀+Ī+X̄>0. Equilibrium isY=A/(1−c+m), so dY/dm=−A/(1−c+m)²<0. Actual imports areM=mA/(1−c+m), whose derivative isA(1−c)/(1−c+m)²>0. The direct increase in import propensity outweighs the fall in income in this standard specification.
hint: Differentiate actual imports mY, not just income.
notes: Uses the standard proportional-import, affine-consumption simple-Keynesian formulation implicit in the question.

stem: IS–LM has C=a+bY, a>0,0<b<1, exogenous I₀,G₀ and money demand L=kY−gr, k,g>0. Nominal money is M₀, initial price P₀. (i) Set up equilibrium equations. (ii) How does a rise to P₁>P₀ affect Y and r?
answer: Y*=(a+I₀+G₀)/(1−b), unchanged by the price rise. r*=[kY*−M₀/P]/g rises by(M₀/g)(1/P₀−1/P₁).
solution: IS is Y=a+bY+I₀+G₀, fixing output regardless of interest because investment is exogenous. It is vertical in the usual(Y,r) plane. LM is M₀/P=kY−gr, or r=(kY−M₀/P)/g. A higher price lowers real money supply and shifts LM upward/leftward. Its intersection with the vertical IS therefore has the same Y and a higher r, with the exact increase given above. There is no investment crowding-out channel in this particular specification.
hint: Notice that no goods-market component depends on interest.

stem: A competitive firm makesY=K^0.25L^0.25. Labour adjusts weekly and capital monthly; wage and capital rental are both10. The question explicitly supplies short-run cost10Y⁴/K̄ and long-run cost20Y². (i) At January’s start output price400: find long-run output and input hires. (ii) At week3 price rises to691.20; fixed capital remains: find short-run output and additional labour for the rest of January.
answer: Using the supplied cost functions: initiallyY10,L100,K100. From week3, Y12 andL207.36, requiring107.36 additional workers per remaining week.
solution: (i) Maximize400Y−20Y². The first-order condition400−40Y0 givesY10. Equal input prices and the symmetric production function implyL=K; Y=√L then givesL=K100. (ii) KeepK100. Supplied short-run variable cost becomes.1Y⁴, withMC=.4Y³. Equate to691.2 to obtainY³1728, henceY12. Production requiresL=Y⁴/K=20736/100=207.36, an increase of107.36 above100. With unchanged conditions this staffing applies in both remaining weeks. Fixed-capital costs, omitted from the supplied short-run formula, do not affect this marginal output choice.
hint: Use the expressly supplied cost functions and hold capital fixed in the third week.
notes: Weekly/monthly accounting is not fully reconciled by the source; computations follow its explicitly provided SR/LR cost formulas, rather than replacing them with another time convention.

stem: A patented drug monopolist facesP=100−X andC=25+X². (i) Find monopoly price and output. (ii) The patent expires, allowing unlimited entry of identical firms with the same cost. Find long-run competitive price, total output and number of firms.
answer: MonopolyX25,P75,profit1225. Free-entry competition: each firmq5, price10, total output90 and18 firms.
solution: Monopoly profit is(100−X)X−25−X²=100X−2X²−25. Its maximum is at100−4X0, givingX25,P75 andprofit1225. With free entry, each active competitive firm must produce at minimum average costAC=25/q+q. Its minimum occurs atq5, whereAC=MC10. Market demand atP10 is90. Therefore18 identical firms each produce5, earn revenue50 equal to cost50 and have zero economic profit.
hint: For free entry use minimum average cost, not monopoly marginal revenue.
notes: Question starts on PDFpage5 and continues on PDFpage2, printedbookletpage8.

stem: Two consumersA,B have identical utilityU=x₁x₂. Endowments areA(1,0),B(0,1). (i) Describe efficient allocations. (ii) Find competitive equilibrium. (iii) Duplicate each type, giving twoA and twoB with the same individual endowments and preferences: find equilibrium allocation.
answer: Efficient allocations giveA(t,t),B(1−t,1−t),0≤t≤1. Equilibrium price ratio1 and each consumer receives(1/2,1/2), both before and after cloning.
solution: For the two-person economy, total stocks are(1,1). Interior efficiency equatesMRS_A=x_A2/x_A1 withMRS_B=(1−x_A2)/(1−x_A1), implyingx_A1=x_A2. The diagonal endpoints are efficient as well: reallocating to improve a zero-utility person necessarily lowers the sole positive-utility holder. Competitive Cobb–Douglas demand spends half of wealth on each good. A wealth isp₁, B wealthp₂. Clearinggood1 requires1/2+p₂/(2p₁)=1, so p₁=p₂; both demand(.5,.5). With two copies of each type, aggregate stocks double to(2,2) and each price-taking person’s wealth/demand at equal prices stays unchanged. Thus all four consume(.5,.5), clearing both markets.
hint: Compute individual half-income demands and then clear markets; cloning scales supply and aggregate demand equally.
